title: Immigration Partnership funding request and Upper Beechwood levy
subtitle: Annual committee night presentations, accessibility and snow clearing, heritage designation deadline, and community announcements on hate reporting and fundraisers.
overview: Council heard from the Waterloo Region Immigration Partnership, which is seeking municipal support after federal funding cuts. Rather than commit money on the spot, Council directed staff to report back later while the area treasurers explore options together {{vote:m3}}. The aim is a shared regional approach to the request.

Council also approved a Special Service/Area Levy for the Upper Beechwood Homes Association properties, starting in the 2027 levy year, and authorized the related agreements {{vote:m4}}. This was passed as part of the consent motion.

In the evening, Council held its annual committee night. Advisory committees on economic development, age-friendly issues, sustainability, Town and Gown, heritage and the creative sector presented their work. Council received the accessibility committee's 2025 highlights {{vote:m5}} and the annual committee night report {{vote:m6}}. The heritage committee noted that listed but undesignated properties come off the municipal register on January 1, 2027. The accessibility committee previewed a coming report on winter sidewalk clearing.

Council also noted a regional anti-hate campaign, We All Belong Here, and an upcoming fundraiser for KidsAbility. The meeting began with a closed session, and the minutes record no public decision from it.

decisions.detail: Council directed staff to report back later on funding opportunities, giving the area treasurers time to explore options for potential support together.

Council approved a Special Service/Area Levy for the listed properties beginning in the 2027 levy year and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign the licence, operating and lease agreements with the homes association, subject to City Solicitor approval.
Council received the 2025 highlights report from the Grand River Accessibility Advisory Committee as information.
Council received the 2025 Committee Night annual report as information.

debate: Delegates said federal cuts removed about a third of the Immigration Partnership's funding, which has limited its community programming. They said the region is a leading final destination for newcomers, and they asked for an annual municipal contribution while also seeking private-sector and other funding.

One councillor asked how a city contribution would directly benefit Waterloo residents rather than the wider region. Delegates said services reach newcomers in every municipality and that the data could be broken out by city.

Another councillor asked how Council should weigh the growing number of funding requests from non-profits as other governments cut back. A delegate declined to rank organizations and pointed to the shared responsibility across levels of government. A councillor said Council should develop criteria for future requests, particularly those covering administrative costs.

The heritage committee described concerns that most of the proposed designations were withdrawn last year after owner objections. It suggested tax relief incentives and options for the Mary Allen neighbourhood before the 2027 register change. Staff said they were working on incentives and aimed for voluntary owner agreement.

The accessibility committee said uncleared sidewalks leave people with disabilities isolated and unable to reach appointments or transit. It said the complaint-based system works poorly for them and suggested an emergency fund, public education and more salt and shovel supplies. A councillor also asked about hybrid council meetings.
